cues.text: Welcome back.
In this class we will work through bulk and shear moduli, stress strain
curves,
critical velocity and combined thermal fluid calculations.
Stretching, squeezing and shearing are different experiments.
Young's modulus Y relates longitudinal stress F/A to fractional length change
the fractional length change within the proportional elastic range.
Bulk modulus B measures resistance to volume change under a uniform pressure
increase.
Because compression decreases volume, B equals the pressure increase/(the
fractional volume change) is positive for an ordinary stable material.
Use consistent signs or use positive compression magnitudes explicitly.
Shear modulus G_s relates tangential stress to shear strain, approximately the
small angular deformation in radians.
A material can resist compression without resisting a lasting static shear:
liquids have a bulk modulus but no equilibrium static shear modulus.
Do not transfer the stretching formula to every kind of deformation.
For a pressure increase of two million pascals and B equals one billion
pascals, the fractional volume change is 0.002, a decrease
of 0.2 percent.
The straight initial part of a tensile stress strain graph obeys Hooke's law;
its slope gives Young's modulus.
A body can still recover its original dimensions beyond the proportional limit
while its response is nonlinear.
The elastic limit is therefore not automatically the end of every straight
section, and the yield point is not a universal sharp feature of all
materials.
Beyond yield, unloading can leave permanent deformation.
In a linear, quasistatic elastic stretch from zero stress, work stored per
original volume is the triangular graph area: one half stress times strain.
A stress of four million pascals with strain 0.002 stores 4000 joules
per cubic metre.
This is energy density, not total energy.
Multiply by the original volume to get energy.
A material being stiff, strong or tough refers to different properties: slope,
limiting stress and energy absorbed before failure should not be confused.
Laminar flow has orderly layers; turbulent flow includes irregular
fluctuations
and mixing.
Reynolds number compares inertial and viscous effects.
For pipe flow, Re equals rho v D/eta using mean speed
v and diameter D.
The critical speed for an assigned critical Reynolds number is Re_critical
eta/(rho D).
The transition threshold depends on geometry, disturbances and the chosen
characteristic length.
A familiar pipe estimate is not a universal constant for every flow.
For water with rho equals 1000 kilograms per cubic metre and viscosity 0.001
pascal seconds in a 0.01 m diameter pipe, take Re_critical equals
2000 as a stated illustrative criterion.
Critical mean speed is 0.20 metres per second.
Doubling diameter halves this estimated speed.
Bernoulli's simple streamline equation assumes steady, incompressible flow
with
negligible viscous losses; continuity can still hold when Bernoulli without
losses is inadequate.
Stokes drag on a sphere requires creeping flow, not arbitrary high speed
turbulence.
For a large open tank draining through a small opening, apply Bernoulli
between
the surface and outlet at the same atmospheric pressure.
Neglect surface speed and losses.
The gravitational height difference h becomes kinetic energy per mass, giving
outlet speed the square root of two g h.
At h equals 0.45 m with g equals 10 metres per second squared, the ideal speed
is 3 metres per second.
The outlet area times speed gives volume flow, not mass flow until density is
included.
If the outlet area is one square centimetre, convert it to 0.0001 m
squared.
Volume flow is 0.0003 cubic metres per second, and water mass flow is
The height will fall in a finite tank, so this is an instantaneous ideal rate
unless the level is maintained.
Adding pressure work again after using Bernoulli would double count an energy
contribution already included.
Real contraction and viscosity reduce the actual outflow compared with this
ideal model.
Heating through a phase change is not one temperature rise calculation.
To turn ice at 10 degrees Celsius into water at 20 degrees Celsius, warm the
ice to zero, supply latent heat of fusion, then warm the liquid.
At fixed pressure a pure material's ideal melting stage changes phase without
changing temperature.
Write an energy ledger before substituting numbers; latent heat has units of
joules per kilogram, not joules per kilogram per kelvin.
Use 0.10 kg ice, ice heat capacity 2100 joules per kilogram
per kelvin, latent heat 334000 joules per kilogram and water heat capacity
4200 joules per kilogram per kelvin.
The three contributions are 2100, 33400 and 8400
J: total 43900 J.
With useful heating power 100 W and negligible losses, time is 439
s.
For heat conduction through two layers of equal area in steady state, thermal
resistances L/(kA) add.
Equal heat current, not equal temperature drop, is the condition linking the
layers.
